parts: Co-ordination is the orderly arrangement of individual and group efforts to provide unity of action in the pursuit of a common goal. It harmonises the activities of different departments (purchase, production and marketing) so that planned objectives are achieved with minimum conflict. Brech: balancing and keeping together the team by ensuring suitable allocation of tasks and harmony among members. Characteristics: it integrates group efforts, ensures unity of action, is a continuous process, all pervasive (a function of managers in all departments and at all levels), is the responsibility of all managers and is a deliberate function. It is called the 'essence' of management.

Significance (increasing with size): growth in size and volume of work means more people and groups working at cross purposes; activities located at different places do not permit close interaction; functional differentiation, division and sub-division of activities and specialisation make co-ordination both more difficult and more important. It helps in reconciliation of goals, total accomplishment of objectives, harmonious relationships and economy and efficiency.

Controlling is evaluating actual performance against planned or standard performance and taking corrective action if necessary. Henri Fayol: 'Control consists in verifying whether everything occurs in conformity with the plan adopted, the instructions issued and principles established.' It includes quality, time and cost, not only quantity. Characteristics: control is a function of management and depends on planning (planning precedes controlling); a continuous process; all pervasive; action is the essence of control; forward looking.

Why control is needed: helps in achieving targets, taking corrective action on time, monitoring and improving employee performance, achieving better coordination and better planning, minimising errors, facilitating decision making and simplifying supervision. Relationship between planning and controlling: planning fixes the goals or standards and controlling checks actual performance with them; without planning control is blind and planning is fruitful only when control is exercised; planning is forward looking (and uses past data) while control is backward looking (compares past performance) as well as forward looking; control brings out shortcomings of planning.

Steps: (1) establishment of standards (quantitative, realistic and attainable, with a range of tolerable deviations); (2) measurement of performance (observation, inspection, reports); (3) comparison of actual performance with standards (equal, more or less); (4) detecting the reasons for deviations; (5) taking corrective action (revision of standards, better selection and training, better motivation) for major deviations outside the permissible range.
